speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN FOR OPENING OF SEAWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition asked the other day whether or not the house would be sitting on June 26, the date of the official opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. I said that if there was agreement I would move a motion today that the house do not sit on Friday, June 26. I find, however, that the motion is such that it is necessary to import into its wording the date when the house will sit.
I have heard it suggested, and I just place this before the house for the moment without comment, that following the opening of the waterway a large number of United States congressmen will be visiting Ottawa on Saturday, June 27. I am not in any way advancing this as a suggestion at the moment, but I know that hon. members are most desirous that every possible day be utilized for the business before us. It might be that later next week consideration may be given, after consultation with the various members of the house, to having the house sit on Saturday, the 27th. The house would then be in a position in which it would not be losing a day's work that week, and at the same time it would make it possible to receive the representatives of the United States congress.
Having said that, with the unanimous consent I move:
That when this house adjourns on Thursday, June 25, it stand adjourned until Monday, June 29.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESULTS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH GRUMMAN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce to the house details of the results of negotiations with the Grumman Aircraft Engineering Corporation of Bethpage, Long Island, New York, in connection with the supply of 10 SA16B aircraft, commonly known as the Albatross, for use by the R.C.A.F. search and rescue service.
The government has decided to award a contract for the supply of these aircraft to the Grumman corporation. The planes are urgently needed for the search and rescue operations of the R.C.A.F. and no other aircraft presently available has the same suitability for recovery at sea or on large water areas as the Albatross. These planes can also be effectively used for freight and supply in the northern areas of Canada, and should prove a valuable acquisition in this regard.
A full examination was made of the possibility of obtaining a licence for the manufacture of this aircraft in Canada, but such a transaction was found to be uneconomic since only 10 aircraft are to be ordered, and even if this quantity was doubled or tripled the cost of Canadian manufacture would still be prohibitive.
Special attention was then given to the working out of production-sharing arrangements, and as a result orders totalling approximately 40 to 50 per cent of the cost of the purchase of these planes will be placed with Canadian manufacturers. The engine which will be installed in the aircraft is the Wright R1820-82, which is being manufactured by Canadian Pratt and Whitney Aircraft Company, Longueuil, Quebec, for our S2F program. This engine can be accommodated in the Albatross aircraft by making a very small engineering change.
Numerous other items made in Canada, such as electronic and navigational items, will be incorporated in the Albatross aircraft, and a portion of the airframe is being subcontracted to Bristol-Aero Industries Limited in Manitoba.
In addition to these arrangements which have been made in connection with the supply of the Albatross aircraft, the Grumman Aircraft Engineering Corporation has agreed to let a subcontract in Canada to

Proposed Legislation
Enamel and Heating Products Limited, Amherst, Nova Scotia, in an amount of approximately $1 million for the supply of a substantial number of components for the S2F aircraft, which the Grumman company is building for the United States navy. The company has also agreed to consider letting additional subcontracts on other work for placement in Canada, but this is, of course, subject to their normal procurement cycle. I am hopeful that these additional orders will amount to a substantial sum over the next few years.
The details of this transaction have been worked out under the recently announced production sharing arrangements made between this government and the government of the United States.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question which, in view of its importance and the fact that I have not been able to give him notice, he may prefer to take as notice. The question is this. In view of the apparent uncertainty in Washington regarding continental air defence, and in view of the downgrading of the Bomarc missile in the latest United States master plan

lor such defence, will the government consider suspending Canadian expenditures on Bomarc and Sage installations until this situation is cleared up?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
subsubtopic: REPORTED DOWNGRADING OF PROGRAM BY U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not accept the preliminary words in the preamble to that question in any way. I rise merely for the purpose of saying that I do not agree with the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition. In so far as the question in general is concerned respecting the Bomarc, I would suggest the Minister of National Defence is the proper minister to answer it.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
subsubtopic: REPORTED DOWNGRADING OF PROGRAM BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may say that I anticipated a question on these lines.
The United States secretary of defence has recommended certain reductions in the number of surface to air missiles planned for use against manned bombers. Briefly, the program involves a reduction in the previously planned deployment of the Bomarc and Nike-Hercules missile batteries and a step-up in the program for the development of an anti-ballistic missile defence. It is not the intention to eliminate one system or the other, but rather to make the best use of both systems since they complement each other. The proposed changes have taken full account of the effective integration of Canadian and United States air defences. These proposed changes do not affect our own defence position or the planned construction and employment of the Bomarc bases in Canada. Only United States bases are affected.
This is a realistic and practical approach to the solution of the problem of the defence of this continent. It conforms with Canadian thinking in that it recognizes, as I have frequently stated, that while the threat from the manned bomber still exists it is a diminishing threat. Therefore expenditures upon any weapons system designed to meet the bomber threat only should be kept within reasonable bounds. The two Canadian Bomarc stations have an important role in the general pattern of continental defence.
We have at all times and at the various official levels been in close touch with the United States authorities. During the past few days I have spoken with Mr. McElroy, the secretary of defence, and his scientific adviser, Mr. Holaday, who made the presentation to the senate armed services committee. These conversations have confirmed our previous knowledge that the proposed redeployment program would not in any way prejudice or make less effective the plans for the defence of Canada that have been agreed upon by our two countries.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
subsubtopic: REPORTED DOWNGRADING OF PROGRAM BY U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Can the minister state whether the press report that the reduction in expenditure recommended in this new defence plan for the Bomarc amounts to over $700 million is accurate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
subsubtopic: REPORTED DOWNGRADING OF PROGRAM BY U.S.
speechtext: There is a very considerable proposed reduction in the amounts to be spent on the Bomarc according to the original deployment plan; but as I have stated, the reductions which are planned will not affect in any way the defence of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture.
In view of flood conditions existing along the Seine river, which have forced the evacuation of some 40 families and are causing extensive damage along its banks in the municipalities of Ste. Anne, Tache and Ritchot, will the minister inform the house regarding any compensations that may be paid to the farmers in the flooded area? Mr. C. Chaput, reeve of the municipality of Ste. Anne, informs me by telephone that the seeded acreage will be a total loss, as the fields are still covered with water.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: MANITOBA-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN SEINE RIVER AREA
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. As far as loss of crops is concerned, awards under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are payable to farmers in the spring wheat area who suffer loss of crop through flooding. In brief, the provision of the act in this regard is as follows. If one third or more of the total cultivated area of the land on six or more adjacent sections of land or river lots cannot be seeded, the farmers owning such land are entitled to an award of $4 per acre with respect to the flooded area. As long as there is an area of six adjacent sections or more, awards can be paid.
If the land has already been seeded it would come under the general provisions as far as loss of property through rain or drought or any other cause is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, questions have been asked in the house during the last few days concerning the passage of United States naval vessels through the Welland canal for celebrations in the upper lakes in connection with the opening of the seaway. As hon. members know, the problem has been that commercial traffic has exceeded expectations and from time to time has been delayed.

For some days friendly discussions have been going on between the two governments, and I am glad to be able to announce that it has now been agreed that only two of these naval vessels per day will be put through the canal on June 22, 23 and 24, and only three each day thereafter up to and including July 1. Furthermore, in some cases where three vessels go through they will be of such dimensions that the lockage required would be the equivalent of that for two of the larger vessels. If it should be found that the locks are not required on any of these days for commercial traffic, the passage of naval vessels will be accelerated. I might add that there has been excellent co-operation from the United States in working out this change of schedule.

Mr. Speaker, on June 11 the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria asked the following question:
Has the minister of mines given any consideration to the proposal by the united mine workers of America that the powers of the dominion coal board be enlarged so that it can act as a coal sales agency?
The answer is yes. This proposal was made to the chairman of the dominion coal board in writing and subsequently verbally by officers of the union. Subsequently the hon. members for Cape Breton North and Victoria and Cape Breton South waited upon me and urged that the government give this proposal most careful consideration. The government has considered the matter very carefully

and cannot accept the suggestion for various reasons, including the following:
(a)	Apparently the coal board would be expected to sell the total production of the Nova Scotia mines at such price as could be obtained, whereas the corporation would carry on the operation of the mines and the government would have to make up the difference between the sales price and the cost of operations.
(b)	The government would have no control over the cost of operation.
(c)	The intervention of the government into the field of private enterprise for the benefit of one corporation would be an unprecedented development which could not be justified.
(d)	The corporation has a well established sales force which works very closely in cooperation with the dominion coal board.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
the purpose of this resolution is to provide on a statutory basis for increases in certain pensions to be paid former civil servants, members of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or their dependants. Hon. members will recall that on July 28, 1958, I informed the house of the provision which the government proposed to recommend to parliament at the 1958 session to increase those pensions based on length of service where the recipients had been retired for a number of years. My review of the government's proposal can be found on pages 2757 to 2759 of 1958 Hansard. What I said on that occasion is equally applicable to the present resolution.
Subsequently increases effective July 1, 1958 in those pensions were authorized by vote No. 667 of Appropriation Act No. 5, 1958, which gave the governor in council the power to prescribe by regulation the terms and conditions under which those increases would be paid to the end of the fiscal year, March 31, 1959. While provision for those increases in respect of the fiscal year 1959-60 has been included in item 123 of the main estimates for the current fiscal year, yet, as indicated in the statement I made on July 28, 1958, the intention of the government was to introduce legislation at this session to provide continuing authority for those increases. As a result of order in council P.C. 1958-1366 of October 2, 1958, which was made pursuant to vote 667, increases in pensions have been paid in respect of the period since July 1, 1958.
During the fiscal year 1958-59 this measure benefited 15,425 cases in the groups of beneficiaries or their dependants which I mentioned earlier, to the extent of approximately $2,364,500.
I am pleased, Mr. Chairman, to say that the responses to the provision contained in the order in council have been very appreciative. I recall that the announcement

which I had the honour of making on July 28, 1958 was well received in the house. The provisions of the bill to follow approval of this resolution are somewhat complicated, since they deal with pensions paid under several acts and involve these different pension formulae. As the bill goes into this matter in some detail, I shall not occupy the time of the house by elaborating further at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this resolution introduced by the Minister of Finance. This house, I believe, will agree entirely with the measure which was taken last year to give some relief to civil servants who had retired on pensions based on salaries which were scaled lower than those which exist now. I was hoping, Mr. Chairman, that the bill which will be introduced would modify some of the provisions which were contained in the order in council of October 2, 1958, to provide moneys for increases in civil servants' pensions. It has been the feeling of this house over some years that if and when this measure was introduced the purpose would be to establish at least a floor for civil service pensions which would enable them to have a good common way of living. If this resolution covers only last year's regulations, it will not in many cases improve the lot of the retired civil servant to the point of bringing his living standard up to that which is general these days.
I am not criticizing the basis of the resolution. However, I hope the Minister of Finance is acting in the light of the experience of the last few months; and by "the past few months" I mean those since July 1, 1958. Having found that the total cost to date has been relatively small, and in view of the fact that this resolution covers only a number of civil servants up to a certain number of years, and it is not an increasing number, I think he should make some effort to improve upon these regulations so that a greater number could benefit, and that the basis should be increased.
As I see it, this resolution will improve the lot of only those civil servants who retired prior to 1953. I must confess that I was guilty of thinking along the same lines. If someone were to refer to some of my speeches on this matter in earlier years they would find that I was also under the impression that provision for those who had retired up to 1953 would just about cover everything. Having seen some of the figures I now realize that this resolution could be extended to cover civil servants having retired up to 1957 and even 1958. I am hoping

that the bill may include some larger contribution and some greater benefits in the smaller pensions of retired civil servants.
This is only the resolution stage. Any information which may be required on the details I think can be obtained on the bill. Once again may I say that this is a welcome measure and that in this bill we hope the minister will do something more than was done last year.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can say that we in this group also welcome the introduction of the resolution which indicates that there is to be some legislation which will have a beneficial bearing on certain of the previous employees of government in varying aspects. It is not our intention at this time to have to have a great deal to say.
As the minister has already pointed out, the bill to be introduced will deal with a number of acts which are at present on the statute books. The resolution foretells of dealings with former civil servants, members of the armed forces and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or their dependants. However, as a result of the indication that such a resolution and bill were going to be introduced, we have been making some investigations in connection with this matter. All we want to say at this moment is that in our estimation there are in the existing acts a great number of discrepancies which need to be resolved, especially with regard to long time employees who have been long time pensioners, and their widows. In particular we feel that there are some discrepancies of a serious nature which must be cleared away with regard to widows of long time pensioners, and that the time is long past when some consideration should have been given to them.
That is all we are going to say at this time. We welcome the resolution and we are looking forward to the bill itself. After we see the bill in all its details and particulars we shall then have more to say.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the annual resolution which precedes the introduction of the annual Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act. It follows the annual review by the special committee appointed by the house to review the statements of the Canadian National Railways, Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited and Trans-Canada Air Lines. That committee sat in the first week of May. It will be recalled that the government was requested to defer the present resolution, or at least defer proceeding with it, and having acceded to this request, Mr. Chairman, it now becomes somewhat urgent that the legislation be quickly proceeded with because it is desirable that it should be completed before the end of this month, for reasons which will be obvious to all members.
Hon. members will be interested to know that in 1952 the form of this annual resolution was changed so as to include the financing of all capital expenditures, whether authorized in that act or in earlier financing and guarantee acts. This procedure has been followed again this year.
The bill to follow the approval of the resolution is divided into three specific parts. The first part is to authorize the Canadian National Railways to incur capital expenditures of up to $348,900,000. The second part authorizes the railway company to make capital expenditures prior to July 1, 1960, to discharge obligations incurred under this act which become due and payable after January 1, 1960 in the amount of $130 million. The third part authorizes the railway company to enter into contracts for the acquisition of new equipment and for general additions and betterments in the amount of $81 million.
To summarize, Mr. Chairman, parliament is being asked to approve financing, either by way of the issue of new securities guaranteed by the government or by way of direct loan, in the amount of $289,900,000. For the convenience of hon. members I would ask permission, Mr. Chairman, to place on Hansard at this point a table giving the details of this sum.

speechtext:
I was just going to come to the conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that it is very confusing to this committee of the whole,

Canadian National Railways which includes members like myself who did not serve on the railways and shipping committee, to find that there is no figure in the resolution before us that can be directly related to the printed evidence that the Minister of Finance has suggested is available in the committee Hansard of this session, on page 215 and following. But I know the Minister of Finance has, as I did in the past, with the consent of the committee tabled some additional information, and the particular paragraphs of the bill do, as it happens, tie themselves in with the evidence before the committee. But I do offer the suggestion from experience that those who draft resolutions of this type might look to ways and means of making it more possible for more than the 30 or more members who have given such great service on the special committee to see something in the resolution which ties in with the evidence that has been given before that committee.
I have looked at the resolution and it does in every respect, except for the figures, follow the pattern of resolutions in previous parliaments. I do, however, think it is appropriate for some of us to comment on certain of the factors which are presented to us at this stage. I was particularly impressed after reviewing, as a non-member, the very voluminous evidence of the railways, air lines and shipping committee in connection with several factors to which I wish to refer briefly. I hope that either at this stage or on second reading or in committee after second reading the Minister of Finance will comment on something which I regard as unusual, and I am referring to the bottom of page 3 of the financial report which the auditors of the C.N.R. made for the year 1958. Paragraph 2 says:
The financial statements for 1958 indicate a deficit of $51.6 million which is the highest recorded deficit since 1938. As explained in the notes to the financial statement-
This is the reference to which I wish to direct the minister's attention. The auditor says:
-on the suggestion of the Minister of Finance a different policy was adopted with respect to the obsolescence of steam locomotives.
All members of the committee may not have examined this balance sheet, but my complaint is this; that to those of us who are laymen it appears as though this figure of 7.1 or 7.2 in the balance sheet of 1957, re steam locomotive obsolescence translated to 1958 has been adjusted in such a way that the deficit of the C.N.R. for 1958 would have been greater to that extent than the figure reported in the press. In other words it would have increased the deficit of the Minister of Finance as announced in his budget

speech by the same amount, had not, in the words of the auditor, a suggestion been made by the Minister of Finance for this $7 million-plus adjustment between the accounts of 1957 and 1958. I hope the Minister of Finance will, at a proper time during the discussion of this report, comment upon this point.
I should also like the minister to indicate to us in the same sequence, since this is a matter relating to capital works and capital requirements, the degree of success or otherwise which has attended the latest bond issue by means of which the C.N.R. is asking the public rather than the minister for funds in a substantial amount to enable the railway to carry out its responsibility. I hope the minister will give us full information on this subject.
I can remember when the hon. member for Greenwood, now Minister without Portfolio, used to have the function which I now have under our parliamentary system, that of examining the proposals of the government and, to the extent that he felt it was in the public interest, questioning some of them and in certain cases criticizing them even though they involved the affairs of a crown company.
I wish to refer to the auditors' statement. I am not knowledgeable about some of these matters which involve high finance, but I had the feeling after reading this report by an experienced international firm of auditors, that they were somewhat alarmed about the rapid growth in the bond indebtedness of this, the largest crown company we have, and in consequence the fixed charges that result from the type of capital borrowing which we are permitting if we approve the proposal which is now before us.
The auditors showed on page 4 of their report to parliament for 1958 that the fixed charges of this railroad-irrespective of the obligation of the government to buy a certain percentage of preferred stock each year, thus introducing new capital into this company, unlike a private company-as a result of this legislation and legislation introduced over the past four or five years and in many years under the previous administration, has resulted in an impost before a profit is earned of the difference between $25.4 million in 1952, after the reorganization of the system, and $46.5 million in 1958. The auditor, to quote his words, said this:
It will be observed that during this period, fixed charges have come close to doubling and there was a particularly marked increase in the years 1957 and 1958, fixed charges going up $5.2 million in 1957 and $9.5 million in 1958.
I only want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that there was no person in the House of Commons who did more to

create an atmosphere of doubt or caution in this respect than his colleague the hon. member for Greenwood, and I hope the Minister of Finance is keeping the debates of previous years in mind when he asks in this resolution for authorization of new capital expenditures not exceeding $348 million for 1959 which, in turn, will increase these fixed charges.
I hope, also, that the minister will give us a little more information concerning capital investment with respect to the trucking operations of the C.N.R. As I say, I did not have the benefit of being a member of the committee, although in the hurried way in which we do these things under the stress of the life we lead, I did peruse the evidence placed before the railways and shipping committee. As X read it I found that for the first time in many years the government's investment in stock of the C.N.R. has risen very substantially. I think the increase amounts to something in excess of $50 million. My closest investigation indicates that a substantial portion of that increase relates to the assumption of certain capital assets of the Hudson bay railway, but as this is a relatively new departure and certainly the greatest rise in government investment or transfer of investment from government back to the Canadian National Railways since 1952 I believe the minister should give us some explanation.
The figures I have indicate that this is a rise since 1952 of $52.9 million. I refer the minister to page 5 of the auditor's report. I have already indicated that the deficit for our largest crown company in 1958 was the largest deficit since 1938, a deficit of $51.6 million; and except for some bookkeeping, the reason for which I have not been properly persuaded, I suggest that this deficit would be an additional $730,000 or $740,000, and I hope the minister will inform us on this particular point.
I have indicated that I was not present in the committee the day this was debated in 1958, but I do not recall that we have ever had any difficulty debating general matters with respect to the Canadian National Railways and I feel it is quite proper at this time to ask the minister what is the present position of this government respecting railway pensions, because he ultimately would have this referred to him from the Minister of Transport. I ask what is the position of the present government, having in mind the long time attitude of the Prime Minister with respect to Canadian National Railways pension increases. I think this is all the more pertinent because of the resolution that was recently disposed of. There was no reference
Canadian National Railways whatever in that resolution to the C.N.R. and I think we should hear from the minister in this respect.
I have in front of me four or five pages of Hansard references to speeches of the Prime Minister in past days as to what should and would be done if he had authority with respect to the enlargement of pensions for retired Canadian National Railways employees. As has been properly said, none of these things that come before us as a parliament could mean too much to us if we did not all have a pretty broad and large confidence in government policy with respect first of all to management and second with respect to the board of directors.
I am not familiar with some of the new directors who have been appointed by order in council by this government. I cast no aspersions upon them, but without any intimate knowledge of the individuals concerned the committee would surely understand that sitting as I do on this side I must have some doubt when I note that one of the replacements on the board was a defeated Conservative candidate and another was a campaign fund collector for the Conservative party. I am just hoping that the government is not looking on this organization, our largest crown company, as another Harrington lake private preserve. I hope that will not be the attitude of this government.
There are one hundred and some odd thousand employees of this railway. They are watching this government very carefully. I want to tell the Minister of Finance and his colleagues that they are very concerned about appointments of this kind to the board which directs the management of this tremendous corporation. I have looked up "Who's Who" as indicative of the achievements of the replacements recommended by this government. I am not going to delay the committee by giving that information. It has always been my view that anything as large as the Canadian National Railways should look very carefully at the manner of appointment of directors of its chief competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway.
In this respect I find two faults. I am an amateur in this game of public finance and business, but as I look at it my first criticism, offhand, would be that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways is too small. I think it is 6 or 7 compared with 25 or 26 on the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I speak of this with some personal knowledge, because I know five or six of the directors of the C.P.R. and three or four of those of the C.N.R. I do know that a C.P.R.

Canadian National Railways director takes his job seriously. He is connected with a great number of other corporations, and in consequence it is his labour to try and bring business, freight and everything else, to the benefit of his company. I am sure that C.N.R. directors now and in the past have a similar obligation in their minds, but I question whether or not the appointment of lawyers, investment dealers and the like-and I remind the committee that I am a lawyer-represents the appointment of adequate replacements.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to one other matter at this point. We have

This has a direct bearing on the kind of legislation we have before us now having to do with capital investment and replacement of old equipment with new that requires less labour. I want to say to the minister and the committee that we are constantly hearing from management of railroads not only in this country but in the United States about featherbedding. In presenting this legislation to us I hope that the minister has had a good look at the standard of efficiency in the operation of the railroad, having regard to the displacement of labour. subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, every year the House of Commons has to deal with a resolution and bill similar to that now before us seeking the authority of parliament for capital or other expenditures running into hundreds of millions of dollars on the part of Canadian National Railways. Sometimes there are questions raised but the legislation is always passed and I think that is as it should be. However, personally I hope that the time is not too far in the future when it will not be necessary for the parliament of Canada to be asked to make these expenditures.
I am not going to make any charges whatsoever but naturally I am somewhat curious with respect to certain aspects of the operations of the Canadian National. I have not been a member of the special committee that deals with the Canadian National but I do have a keen interest in the operations of the railway. Canadian National Railways is a publicly owned system. In the past 26 years I have travelled from the Pacific coast to the Atlantic coast or from the Pacific coast to Ontario so often that I cannot possibly remember the number of times I have made the trip. My travelling has been both on the Canadian National and on the Canadian Pacific, and in making these long trips I have had a great many conversations with locomotive engineers, firemen, brakemen, passenger and freight conductors. These conversations have resulted in my present curiosity. I sincerely hope that either now or on second reading the Minister of Finance will answer
Canadian National Railways certain questions I have in mind arising from my conversations over the past 26 years with the men who are on the job and also because of the number of letters I have received in the past week as a result of the publicity given to the hearings before the special committee of the house which investigated the Canadian National.
My main question is, what was the relationship and attitude of the previous government with respect to the C.N.R.? If the minister cannot answer that, what is the attitude and relationship of the present government with respect to the C.N.R. as a publicly owned system compared with the Canadian Pacific, a privately owned railway? Does the government support the morale of the employees of the publicly owned system? Is there any direction at all from the present government to the Canadian National to operate in the most efficient way it possibly can and do the best job it possibly can? I should like very much to have an answer to that because from what I have been told by C.N.R. employees there is either a peculiar situation on that railway involving direct or indirect sabotage or else there is not sufficient backing of the publicly owned company. I have yet to find a person operating trains on the Canadian National, locomotive engineers, firemen, freight conductors or passenger conductors who will not say that the Canadian National could beat the blazes out of the Canadian Pacific on time from the Pacific to the Atlantic. But, Mr. Chairman, the schedules make the running time of the Canadian National a little bit slower than that of the Canadian Pacific. Why is this so?
The Canadian National has not the steep grades of the privately owned line. Those who do the running say that they could beat the privately owned line by hours. We, the people, own the Canadian National so why do we not do what all the conductors, engineers and dispatchers say can be done? If what I am told by businessmen is correct, and I think it is, then speed is money in so far as transportation matters are concerned. Who sets the scheduled time of passenger and freight trains on the Canadian National? Why is it, especially with regard to the Rocky mountain section where there are practically no grades at all compared with the Canadian Pacific grades, that the freight situation is the way it is?
I say, Mr. Chairman, it is curious, and I hope the minister can tell us why that situation prevails, and whether or not there are any controls being placed upon the Canadian National to limit the time in which those trains, either passenger or freight, can traverse the country from ocean to ocean. I am

Canadian National Railways very glad the Postmaster General is here. I am not speaking of the past two or three years because I have made no check during that time, and I want that clearly understood. I do know that previous to that I have actually seen Her Majesty's mail being transferred from Canadian National trains to Canadian Pacific trains at the first junction point, and yet the Canadian National train would reach Vancouver three hours before the Canadian Pacific train to which the mail was transferred. I have actually seen that happen, but not within the last two or three years. Does that situation still apply, or does it apply in similar circumstances across our entire transcontinental system?
There are other questions that come to mind. We have just recently opened a $11 million post office in Vancouver. Well over $1 million, I know, must have been spent on the tunnel from the post office to the Canadian Pacific station-it might well be $2 million, including equipment. Is there any reason why no tunnel was constructed to the Canadian National and Great Northern station, the Canadian National carries mail across Canada and the Great Northern to the United States? Is there any reason why there is only a tunnel to the Canadian Pacific station and not to the Canadian National? There are many questions. The Canadian National, I believe, is known as one of the greatest transportation systems in the world. We are certain it could be a lot better, so why is it not allowed to improve?
I have travelled Canadian Pacific for the last few trips I have made between Vancouver and Ottawa. It is amazing, Mr. Chairman, when you get into a discussion with travellers who have travelled on both lines to hear them say they will only travel by Canadian Pacific. I usually ask them why, and they will say that the Canadian Pacific has the dome cars and the Canadian National has not. Why, in the competition for passenger traffic and with far less tunnels than the Canadian Pacific has, has the Canadian National not the modern equipment? I am told that the Canadian National is losing out on passenger traffic because they have not the equipment. The Canadian National would not have to spend anywhere near the money on tunnel changes that the Canadian Pacific has, and yet they have not the type of equipment that the privately owned line has.
Is it deliberate? Is there any influence brought to bear or is it poor management? There must be answers somewhere to these questions which are posed to me either directly in conversation or by correspondence. I do not know the answers. All I do know is that year after year we have to vote hundreds of millions of dollars for the

Canadian National. There is no objection at all. Could the amount be reduced by greater efficiency? Could the amount be reduced by a speedier service? Could the amount be reduced if the Canadian National were permitted to operate on an absolutely competitive basis? All the information and evidence I have would lead me to believe that it could.
I hope that the minister, either now or on second reading, will make clear the policy and attitude of this government toward the operation of the Canadian National. Are they allowed a free hand in competition? Are they allowed a free hand on service and on equipment? As soon as the minister can give us answers to these questions, then we will know where to place the responsibility, either upon the government or on the management of the Canadian National.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of delaying this resolution unduly. There are, however, a number of points that I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and of the government as well. They arise, not only out of the statement made by the minister but out of other extraneous matters, some of which have been dealt by my colleague the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
I have listened with interest to the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Not being on the other side of the house any longer, I have no intention of stating what the policy of the former administration was with reference to directing or not directing the affairs of Canadian National Railways. The minister, I am sure, will be able to give the position of the government if he chooses to reply to the query made by the hon. member.
However, I rose to deal with a number of other matters. In making his introductory statement the minister said that the bill divided itself into three parts. First, the bill authorizes the C.N.R. to incur an expenditure up to $348 million. Next, it authorizes the C.N.R. to make expenditures prior to July 1, 1960 in an amount of $130 million. Third, it authorizes the C.N.R. to enter into contracts for new equipment in the amount of $81 million, I believe. This information prompts me to discuss a matter which I have already brought to the attention of the government and which arises out of the establishment of the royal commission on transportation.
While no indication has yet been given by the Prime Minister or by the Minister of Transport as to the likelihood of the royal commission inquiring into certain aspects of the operation of the Canadian National Railways other than the broad terms of reference

which have already been announced, it seems to me that some consideration ought to be given to that matter. It seems to me that, because of the position in which Canadian National Railways finds itself at the moment, active consideration ought to be given by the government, not to going into the whole financial aspect of the railway but at least to going into some of the aspects which fall to be determined by a royal commission of this nature on transportation.
I can think of a number of matters to which consideration might be given. It seems to me that the commission might well look at the C.N.R. finances; I refer to the overall capitalization. My friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River spoke about the deficit position and the increase in certain costs such as fixed assets. He drew the attention of the committee to the fact that over a period of years these costs have gone up considerably because of inflation, increase in the costs of materials, increase in the cost of equipment itself and also the dieselization program of the C.N.R. It also seems to me that the commission might well look into the terms under which the government capital should be provided.
I also wonder whether the time has not arrived to examine into the whole question of the financing of Canadian National Railways and to take another look at the capital structure of Canadian National Railways. As the committee knows, this was done in part by the former royal commission on transportation which made a substantive recommendation having to do with the recapitalization of the C.N.R., which recommendation was later implemented by the then government.
Is it necessary to give consideration to a matter of this kind at this time? I believe it is necessary. I do not think the minister will disagree with what I am saying, at least in its broad aspects. Again I want to make it clear that it is not possible to make a study of matters which have been entrusted to the royal commission and to go into the whole matter of the financing of the Canadian National Railways. However, I think there are aspects which might well be studied within the broad terms of the commission's reference.
May I now pass to another matter. The minister said that this bill deals with the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways. I must say to him that I view with concern the appointment of an auditor for the year 1960 other than the firm which has given such excellent service to the Canadian National Railways over a period of years. I view it with concern for more than one reason. In the first place, I am informed
Canadian National Railways -and I believe this to be so-that the present auditors, George A. Touche and Company were not given notice that they were to be replaced by another firm. In the second place, I view this matter with concern because it was my experience when I sat on the other side of the house that the operations of the Canadian National Railways are such that they are to be found not only from one end of this country to the other but also in the United States as well. The Canadian National Railways have always argued that it is difficult if not impossible for an auditor to do the kind of job that should be done unless that auditor has subsidiaries or branches in the United States as well as in the large cities of Canada.
George A. Touche and Company have such subsidiaries. The Canadian Naional Railways operates a number of lines in the United States and, I need hardly add, lines in every part of Canada. The auditor who has been appointed for the year 1960-and I say this without wanting to reflect on him personally in the slightest degree-is, as the minister knows, a former defeated candidate of the Progressive Conservative party in one of the Montreal ridings. I do not want to pursue the matter unduly but I fear-and I shall have something to say about this subject a little bit later on-the danger of introducing politics into a railway of this magnitude.
I come back again to the point of the importance of and the necessity for an auditor of a crown corporation such as the Canadian National Railways having offices in the various regions of Canada, particularly a crown corporation with assets such as those possessed by the Canadian National Railways which include railways, airlines-I take it that the appointment of the auditors for 1960 also covers Trans-Canada Air Lines; if I am mistaken I stand to be corrected-telecommunications, transportation facilities, hotels; all of which, added up, come to many hundreds of millions of dollars; I believe the amount is well over $3 billion. Those are substantial assets. It would seem to me that the person who is going to audit such a corporation should at least have had some experience in that field. George A. Touche and Company have had a great deal of experience. I can remember that on another occasion many years ago, when there was a change of government there was also a change of auditors. On that occasion-and now I speak, of course, only from memory-the firm appointed was one which had offices all over the country and also in the United States.

They have international connections.

I deprecate also, Mr. Chairman, the appointment of some of the members of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. Again I do not want to reflect on the person of any of these individuals, but I do feel it is a mistake when on a board of this importance men seem to be appointed rather because of their political affiliations than because of their business competence or business connections. I refer now to the successor to Mr. Ralph Brenan. I would like to put on the record a portion of an editorial which appeared in the Fundy Fisherman of January 28, 1959. The editorial is entitled, "Name Political Leader to C.N.R. Board", and reads as follows:
There will be widespread concern throughout the Atlantic region at the replacement of Ralph B. Brenan, one of the region's most outstanding business leaders, as director of the Canadian National Railways. It is well known that the difficulties of the C.N.R. are very great and require the most experienced management to surmount. Mr. Brenan brought to the board of management gifts of understanding of regional problems that are widely recognized as being of exceptional calibre.
The announcement from the office of Hon. George Hees, Minister of Transport, said that Mr. Brenan's term of office has expired. His replacement, W. Gerald Stewart, Q.C., is a past president of the New Brunswick Progressive Conservative Association.

speechtext:
I continue:
It has long been recognized that there should be a minimum of political weight given to appointments to a board of directors such as the C.N.R. and that business management qualifications are of paramount concern. The great seaports of Halifax and Saint John, faced with growing difficulties, had, in Mr. Brenan, a representative on the board thoroughly intimate with the problems of freight movements as they affect ocean shipping. His place will be difficult to fill.
Then I come to the final part of this editorial:
In the loss of the services, guidance and knowledge of Ralph B. Brenan, the C.N.R. has been given a severe blow. In a time of economic recession when the most efficient and capable management and direction is important, it is particularly unfortunate that his outstanding business ability is lost to a public board of such importance to the well-being of the Atlantic region.
Saint John citizens, who have for many years intimately known Mr. Brenan's exceptional gifts as a community leader and selfless devotion to public duties, will especially regret that his services are no longer available to an organization which is so important in many ways to the seaport.
Those are not my views; those are the views of this newspaper.
Then there is another appointment which has been made to replace that of Mr. Parker

from the province of Manitoba. The minister also will correct me if I am wrong in this respect. My information is that the person who has succeeded Mr. Parker has far more information and is far more competent in affairs concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway Company than in those concerning the Canadian National.

Yes, I understand that is the case, Mr. Chairman. However, this appointment has been made to succeed that of Mr. Parker's. If that is the case, as I have indicated, then I believe that that is not a good thing for the adequate operation of the Canadian National Railways.
There are a number of other matters that I might go into, but I desire to mention but one, and that has to do with the lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. Unfortunately I am not in a position to place the facts on the record concerning that because we have not been given the information in that respect that I think we should have had. It was the practice of the former administration when asked questions of this nature to place on Hansard on orders of the day or on other occasions the position in so far as the C.N.R. lay-offs were concerned. I remember when I occupied a position on the other side that I was taken to task on more than one occasion by the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre because of the lay-offs which took place from time to time, and they were not nearly as great or substantial as they have been during the course of the years 1958 and 1959. As I say, I was taken to task because of lay-offs arising out of the information that I gave on the orders of the day.
But we have not been furnished such information. Questions have remained unanswered, or questions have been answered by indicating that the information could be obtained in committee. This information was not obtained in committee. Nonetheless, it seems to me that it should have been given in the house. The fact is that we have not received a comprehensive up to date statement about the lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways although we know that they are pretty substantial. It would seem to me, that before this bill passes the minister should give some indication of what these are.
There are, I am informed, employees of the Canadian National Railways having in some cases seniority of 35 and 40 years who have been laid off. Is there any reason for

this? Is it because the freight and passenger business of the Canadian National Railways has declined to the point where it has been necessary to do this? If that is the case, then I think the minister should give a full and frank statement of what the position is in all the regions of Canada, and then we will know the answer to that question.
I desire at this time to bring these points to the attention of the committee because I feel that before this measure passes they should be given consideration not only by the government but also by the minister who speaks for the government on this occasion.

Mr. Chairman, there is one problem in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways in Newfoundland which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time, and through him to his colleagues in the government. The railway service in Newfoundland is different, I think, from that in the other provinces in that it serves both inland and coastal settlements. The coastal settlements are served by coastal boats which are operated by the railway. In addition, the railway operates ships which transfer freight from mainland ports to ports in Newfoundland.
The problem I wish to describe to the minister is one which concerns freight claims. If an accident happens to a train, and goods in transit are damaged or lost the person to whom the goods are consigned can submit a claim, and that claim may be recognized and paid. If a ship transporting goods for the C.N.R. from mainland ports to Newfoundland ports runs ashore or meets with an accident, the same process is followed-the person to whom the freight is consigned can submit a [DOT]claim and obtain compensation in respect of damaged or lost goods. But the people in
Canadian National Railways the coastal regions who are served by coastal boats do not have this privilege. A person who loses freight or whose goods are damaged because a coastal boat runs ashore or meets with an accident cannot obtain satisfaction of a claim for loss or damage, the reason being that these coastal boats operated by the C.N.R. are exempted by the water carrier act. Because of these circumstances there is discrimination between people who live inland and people who live on the coast and who are served by the same company. It seems to me that the answer is to have the coastal boats excluded from the terms of the Water Carriage of Goods Act in this respect, and I would ask the minister to look into this matter and see if something can be done about it.
