subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is an interesting question from the hon. member from Kenora-Rainy River. If his assertion is that anyone who is a defeated candidate or who has at any time been a defeated candidate is unfit to hold public office, then I think he is introducing something which will, on reflection, occur to him as being a dangerous principle, because there are quite a few people in the government service who have at one time or another been unsuccessful candidates. What is sauce for the goose must be sauce for the gander. I presume the hon. member would reconcile that situation with what he said by insisting that he was only referring to those who were defeated Conservative candidates.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: No, I am referring to the biggest crown corporation-the C.N.R.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Apparently it is all right if those who preceded us appointed their defeated candidates to public office, but it becomes all wrong when the present government appoints to public office distinguished and worthy citizens who happen to be defeated candidates-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: A point of order. The minister has asserted that the previous government appointed former defeated candidates. Who were they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I could mention a considerable number.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: To the C.N.R.? That is what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am speaking
about government appointments in general. Surely, if the principle is good it must be a sound principle of general application. I do not hold with the principle just put forward by hon. members opposite. I do not think the fact that a man has been a candidate for public office-whether he has been successful or unsuccessful in obtaining it-is any disqualification for public service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
If he has the
proper qualifications for public service, surely his candidature should not be allowed to stand in his way, regardless of the party whose candidate he was. If this applies in the case of one party I think hon. members opposite should be fair enough to recognize that it applies to persons who have been political candidates for parties other than their own.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: It has been too conspicuous in this one big crown company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me make it
clear that there have been four or five vacancies which have occurred in the ordinary course on the board of the C.N.R. since this present government came to office two years ago. I referred, in my question to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, to two members of that board who had been reappointed by the present government. I note that the hon. member has no fault to find with those reappointments, but when the present government appoints others he has fault to find at once.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Just alarmed and worried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me say that
the government considers these new appointments to be of men of high accomplishment and seasoned experience who are capable of making a notable contribution to the direction of the affairs of the Canadian National system as members of the board of directors. I think we have been fortunate in the quality of the men we have been able to appoint to the board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Can I ask the minister
a question? Would he just describe the past connections of these men that might be translated into business for the C.N.R., or their experience other than being a lawyer or an investment dealer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
You will note that that question comes from the side of the house that disclaims any idea of introducing personal considerations into this question. Here we are asked to sit down and rake over the whole personal story of every one of our appointees, and yet we are told: Oh no, this is not prompted by any personal consideration.
The present set-up of the C.N.R. with a seven-man board was devised by the former government. We have made no change in that. It was decided by the former government, supported by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, that it should be small rather than a large board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In that, perhaps I was
wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The present government did away with the commission form of management of the C.N.R. in favour of a small board of directors. We have made no change in that respect whatever. I expect in the light of what we have heard this afternoon that if we had enlarged the board of directors we would have been told that we had enlarged it for the purpose of appointing Conservatives to it. We have made no change whatever but have left the board precisely as it was.

The board has been set up from the beginning on a different basis from that of the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific railway for reasons the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River recognized in his remarks this afternoon. The nature of appointments has been different because of the difference in the size of the board and the fact that in one case you have a private corporation and in the other a public corporation. Those whom we have been fortunate enough to enlist in the public service by accepting appointments to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways are highly fit and qualified men who will give important and valued service on the board of directors of the C.N.R. system. The same applies to the other appointment which was mentioned and which can more properly be discussed on the bill.
Let me now deal with a point raised by the hon. member for Laurier who spoke about the present royal commission and suggested that it ought to examine as well the capitalization of the Canadian National Railways system. I would recall to his mind that the royal commission is a commission on railway freight rates and the scope of the commission does not include inquiry into the capitalization of the C.N.R. system. May I remind him, however, of the fact-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The terms of reference are pretty broad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. I speak subject to correction but it had not occurred to me that the terms of reference contained any provision that would include under any of the paragraphs an inquiry into the capitalization of the national system.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister would permit a question at this stage. My recollection is that a portion of it had to deal with railway transportation and the effect on railway transportation. I do not have the terms before me. That is why it struck me, however, that perhaps it would be possible to give consideration to some aspects of railway financing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I remind the committee, Mr. Chairman, that under the present financial provisions inscribed in the statute of this parliament the C.N.R. sells to the Minister of Finance each year preferred stock equivalent to 3 per cent of the gross earnings of the railway. Last year that involved a purchase on the part of the Minister of Finance of $21 million of the 4 per cent preferred stock of the corporation and this year it will involve a purchase by the Minister of Finance of $22.7 million of that preferred stock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Is that realistic?
Canadian National Railways

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is what the statute requires.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I know; introduced by the former government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. That is what we are following obediently. That is the will of parliament.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: You have taken no decision to change it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This bill makes no provision in this respect and no other legislation on this subject has been indicated for the present session.
Let me quickly run through the other points raised by hon. members who asked for information. The hon. member for Vancouver East asked about the schedules of operation. This is entirely a matter within the power of the management of the Canadian National Railways system. It would be intolerable if the government or parliament interfered and told the C.N.R. system in detail how it should operate the trains or whether a transcontinental train should cut half an hour off its running time. It is obvious that this is clearly a matter falling within the scope of management and it would be highly improper for the government to interfere in the details of operations of that kind.
As to raising questions of this nature may I point out to the hon. member that that is the function and purpose that is served by the appointment annually of the special committee of the house because there hon. members, including at least one member from his own party, attended and asked a great many questions about operations. If he did not ask this question then perhaps the hon. member could put it on the list of questions to be asked the next time the officials of the system come before a parliamentary committee for questioning.
I was asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River concerning the increase in the government investment in the national system. Here may I point out that apart from several small items the increase in the capital investment by the government of Canada is accounted for by two large items. The first is the investment in the Hudson Bay railway which has been transferred to Canadian government railways; the amount is $34,682,534.80.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That was under the present minister's regime?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, in 1958. The next item is the investment in the northwest communications system which was transferred to the Canadian National Railways; the amount is $17,833,075.52.

Canadian National Railways

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Had there been any
similar increase in the previous five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will make inquiries on that subject, Mr. Chairman.
A question was asked about the C.N.R. loan. I thought I had reported in the house already on this. On May 15 last the Canadian National Railways issued $150 million of 5 per cent bonds. These were duly sold, being $60 million of 1968 maturity and $90 million of 1977 maturity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe I inquired about the effective rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There was a 5 per cent coupon. The 1968 maturity was sold at $98.75 to yield about 5.18 per cent. The 1977 maturity was sold at $98 to yield approximately 5.17 per cent to maturity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Would the minister permit a question at this time. I recall from my experience that when dealing with the large annual financial volume of requirement for the C.N.R. it has been customary for the government to underwrite it until such time as the bond market seemed to be propitious for the Canadian National Railways to go itself into the normal courses of the investment field for funds on a longer term. What would be the position at the moment with respect to the requirements contemplated in this bill which I believe the resolution says are approximately $348 million? What would be the picture for the next twelve months if the C.N.R. could not go into the financial market and get it own bonds on a long term basis? What are we really committing ourselves to in approving of this capital expenditure in so far as interest rates are concerned?
The other question I have in mind is this. To whom would the minister or alternatively to whom would the C.N.R. apply for getting these large amounts of capital funds? I think it is relevant now because we have to consider the present market. I did not feel the minister answered me very properly this afternoon when I gave to him the benefit of what was admittedly my own arithmetic after looking at the offer the minister had made for a new $200 million government of Canada loan requirement. What would the position be in connection with these capital requirements of the C.N.R.? Is it correct that if they needed money for only nine months and if they had a nominal interest rate on the bonds at 2J per cent and they were sold at a 2 point discount, anybody paying a 50 per cent income tax rate would find that that would be equivalent to 8.2 per cent compared with a par offering for nine months for the same amount of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Obviously the
hon. gentleman is wandering far from the subject matter before us and from the real purport of the inquiry he directed to me. He knows quite well, I am sure, that Canadian National Railways borrow money from the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
If they cannot get it
from the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This has been
the practice for a long time. It certainly was the practice before we came into office because when we came into office we found that Canadian National Railways had borrowed from my predecessor as minister of finance- I speak now subject to correction as to the amount-something like $300 million. That was the indebtedness of Canadian National Railways to the former minister of finance when we came into office two years ago. That is the position. The first place of borrowing by Canadian National Railways is from the Minister of Finance, and periodically the company goes into the market to borrow money there by an issue of bonds guaranteed by the government. Canadian National Railways went into the market with the largest issue of bonds in its history in January 1958-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Three hundred million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: -and recently, as I have indicated, went in for another issue.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Another big one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member asked me what the rate would be for the next 12 months. I cannot predict the rate, Mr. Chairman. If I were able to do that I would be able to do something that I am sure nobody in Canada professes to be able to do at this moment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I assure the
minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I continue, Mr. Chairman? I am trying to answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister allow me to ask a question-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I finish what I am saying?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: -in this context, may I say that the minister was probably justified-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
-in interpreting my remarks in the way he did. What I said was, would he confirm to this committee that if funds were not available outside-

The Depuiy Chairman: Order. If the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wishes to ask a question, perhaps he will wait until the minister has finished.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member asked that question before, in fact, several questions, and I am endeavouring to answer them. If I may continue, the hon. member will hear such answer as I am able to give him. It may not be the one he wishes but it will be such as I am able to give him.
This is the practice that has been followed. It is the practice that is in effect at the present time. What the bill will do will be to follow the usual provisions that have been in effect now for many years governing the financing operations of Canadian National Railways in this respect.
The next question I was asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was in relation to trucking operations on the part of Canadian National Railways. I draw his attention to page 69 of the proceedings of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government for May 4 where he will see that subject reviewed by the president of Canadian National Railways. He indicated on that page the circumstances under which the management proposes to enter on a trucking operation, saying that they needed to do so to be able to maintain their competitive position. If the hon. member will look further at page 221 of the proceedings he will see the amount given there in the statement tabled by the president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Was it $15 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is $15 million for investment in capital stock of Canadian National Transportation Limited.
The final matter on which hon. members asked me questions concerned a difference in relation to a bookkeeping item amounting to something over $7 million. This also was discussed in the committee. The hon. member for Laurier raised it there. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will find it dealt with at pages 195 and 196 of the committees proceedings. The hon. member for Laurier introduced it at some considerable length and Mr. Gordon made the following comment on it:
This whole affair arose out of a difference of opinion between technicians, in a sense. Our accountants-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: You advised this. Are you the technician?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. member will wait until I have read the whole answer I think it will be quite clear to whom Mr. Gordon refers.
66968-9-300
Canadian National Railways
This whole affair arose out of a difference between technicians, in a sense. Our accountants, supported by our legal department, felt that the entry for depreciation, as you have described it, was the proper way to handle this. When the matter reached the Minister of Finance, in terms of its being an item which should add to our deficit for that year, he took the position that it was not a proper entry as contemplated by the legislation. As I say, there was a difference of opinion. That difference of opinion was referred to the Department of Justice, and the Department of Justice gave a legal ruling, supporting the position of the Minister of Finance. In the light of that, there was nothing else we could do, and there was nothing else the Minister of Finance could do, because the ruling was given in the terms of an interpretation of the legislation that existed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: With respect to the concluding remarks of the Minister of Finance, probably I should not have interrupted him with some vehemence, but does he recall that I quoted a very authoritative source saying that he was the one who advised this change? I do not find that there is too much departure in the evidence he has just read to the committee from page 195.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I can clarify that if there is anything further to be added. When this matter came to my attention it was quite clear what the views of Canadian National Railways were, but we are not necessarily bound by them. My accounting advisers took the opposite view and in view of the difference of opinion the matter was referred to the Department of Justice for a ruling with the result that Mr. Gordon indicated in his testimony to the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
If the Department of
Justice had not so ruled, the deficit as reported to the house in April would have been more than $7 million larger than was reported?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is the approximate figure. I think it was just over $7 million.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There are a few questions I should like to ask. My hon. friend has referred to the fact that the C.N.R. has two methods of financing its operations. One is by direct loan from the government of Canada and the other by borrowings from the Canadian people. He has referred to an issue of $150 million on May 15, I think it was, and I believe the rate of interest was 5 per cent. Is that the correct rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct. That was the coupon rate on both maturities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Are these loans from the public undertaken by the C.N.R. the result of agreement on the part of the government or the Minister of Finance?

Canadian National Railways

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
What kind of
agreement?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the Minister of Finance concur in the decision to make a public borrowing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The timing of the issues by Canadian National Railways is, of course, a matter for prior discussion between the management of the national system and the Minister of Finance because the Minister of Finance is required, pursuant to legislation contained in this type of bill, to guarantee the issue.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is what I thought. Would I be correct in saying that one of the reasons for the decision to have this borrowing of $150 million undertaken was the failure of the $300 million issue that came out in January of 1958, I believe?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is entirely wrong for the hon. member to suggest there was any failure in connection with that January, 1958 loan. It was a very successful loan and was oversubscribed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The Bank of Canada report says it was accompanied by softness in its relationship with the commercial banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The loan was substantially oversubscribed. We were very pleased with the result of this offer of Canadian National bonds.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance says that this was a very successful loan, and he will of course recall that it had very considerable difficulty at the outset.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The minister says, no; I think he will find that is the case. The governor of the Bank of Canada, at page 24 of his report, said that it involved initially a large increase in bank loans to security dealers, which is another way of saying that the loan did not meet with immediate public response. Certainly, the fact that a year later these bonds had a market value of between 85 and 89 is an indication of their reception and also of the state of the bond market at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Not at that time, no.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
A year later, I said, these bonds were worth around 85 or 89.
One of the reasons suggested for the investment of some of the trust funds of the unemployment insurance commission in

this particular Canadian National 4 per cent bond issue of $300 million was to encourage the public to participate in this borrowing which I say was not, in spite of what the minister says, a success at the beginning. What I want to ask the minister is this: Did the unemployment insurance commission investment committee decide to invest $15 million in what I say was, at the outset, an unsuccessful issue or certainly an issue that was not readily responded to, with the minister's knowledge? Was the minister aware of the decision to make this investment by the unemployment insurance investment committee, of which the governor of the Bank of Canada acts as chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member is entirely wrong in the statements that he is making. He keeps on talking about the reception of the loan. The reception of the loan in January, 1958 was most cordial. I might say that the loan was very heavily oversubscribed. It was almost a record oversubscription, and that on the largest loan ever offered by Canadian National Railways.
Now, if the hon. gentleman talks about any drop in the quoted market value of bonds since then, he could take other examples as well and he could compare them as I had occasion to do not many weeks ago in this house. There was a substantial drop in the market value of all kinds of government bonds in this country in the years 1955-1957, bigger drops than have occurred since.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Not like the one now!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I shall be glad to go back and put those on the record again if it gives any comfort to hon. members to contemplate this subject.
But I come to the question asked by the hon. member. The Minister of Finance does not stand peering over the shoulders of the investment committee of the unemployment insurance commission to supervise, day by day, their financial transactions. These are highly competent men, I am sure the best available for this very important service. Whatever investment they made at that time I am sure was the kind of investment that would have been advised by any other competent person under the circumstances existing then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: No one quarrels with the competence of the governor of the Bank of Canada or the members of the investment committee of the unemployment insurance commission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: If the minister does not look over their shoulders.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The question of their competence only beclouds the issue. I say again that this loan had great difficulty in getting under way, and the decision of the investment committee of the unemployment insurance commission to invest trust funds, largely the contributions of workers and employers in this country, was taken at a time when this issue was having the difficulty which I have mentioned, and which the minister denies but I think the fact will support what I am saying, as indeed does the report from the governor of the Bank of Canada which I have read.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: He is referring to the after market, which is a different thing altogether.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I also referred to the after market. A year later the value of the bonds was between 85 and 89. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATIONS, PROVIDE FOR MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
purpose of this resolution is to permit the introduction of a bill to extend the Farm Improvement Loans Act for a further lending period and to amend the act in certain other respects.
This legislation was originally enacted in 1944 and came into force on March 1, 1945. The act was designed to encourage the granting by banks of intermediate and short term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms and for the improvement of living conditions thereon. The purposes for which farmers may obtain loans are many and varied and include loans to assist in financing the purchase of agricultural implements, livestock, agricultural equipment, farm electric systems and irrigation systems and to assist in financing the construction or alteration of farm buildings and improvements or developments of a farm, such as fencing, drainage, irrigating, breaking, and similar projects.
These loans are made by the chartered banks under a guarantee provided by this legislation. The government's liability to a bank is limited to 10 per cent of the aggregate

principal amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans made by a bank during a lending period. This liability has also been limited to a total lent by all banks during a lending period of $300 million. The maximum amount of a farm improvement loan is presently set at $5,000 and the interest rate is five per cent simple interest. Repayment terms of loans are for varying periods up to 10 years, depending upon the amount borrowed and the purpose for which the loan was obtained.
Loans under the act during 1958 totalled 70,278 in number and $90,539,743 in amount borrowed. This represents an increase in lending of approximately $20 million over the amount lent during each of the preceding three years. Repayments during the year amounted to $76,946,506.
As I have indicated, lending during 1958 was substantially larger than in each of the preceding three years, and for the months of January, February and March, 1959, a further increase has occurred over the corresponding period in 1958. In these three months the sum of $14,707,086 was borrowed in 1959 as against $10,436,991 in the same period in 1958. This represents an increase of almost 41 per cent over last year, so that lending during 1959 may be expected to reach a record volume.
Since the inception of the act to December 31, 1958, that is to say 15 years ago, a total of 723,675 loans have been granted for $813,499,097. Repayment of loans to December 31, 1958 amounts to $675,433,667, which is approximately 83 per cent of the amount borrowed. Accumulated losses under the guarantee since inception of the lending to December 31, 1958 amount to $835,772, of which $60,614 has been recovered. Therefore the loss ratio on $813 million lent is less than one-tenth of one per cent.
The figures give some indication of the credit service which has been rendered to Canadian agriculture through this legislation. The credit has been available and utilized in all provinces, and for the information of the committee I might place on the record a table indicating the extent of the lending by provinces for the years 1957 and 1958. It might meet the convenience of hon. members if it were incorporated in Hansard at this point in my remarks.

It will be noted that there has been an average increase in the amount lent in all provinces of 30.4 per cent in 1958 over 1957.
Specifically, the purpose of the present resolution is to permit the introduction of a bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act in order to achieve the following objectives:
1.	To include beekeepers as qualified borrowers under the act. At present it is not possible for persons who have a principal occupation of beekeeping to obtain loans under the act. It is felt that lending should be made available for such persons.
2.	To increase the maximum loan allowable under the act to $7,500. This is considered warranted by reason of the additional capital requirements for farming in this mechanized age. The present limit on any one loan is $5,000. A loan of $7,500 would, of course, be beyond the repayment ability of the average farmer over a four-year term, but the increased amount could be utilized by banks in the case of large operators.
3.	To extend the provisions of the act for a further lending period. Lending since inception has been done within certain lending periods and the latest of such periods expired March 31, 1959. It is proposed to have the new lending period extend from April 1, 1959 to June 30, 1962. Although most lending periods have been for exactly three years in the past the proposed expiry date of the new period would make it possible to amend the act to set up a new period at a more appropriate time than is the case when a period ends March 31st. Although the latest lending period under the act terminated on March 31 last, I might say that the lending operations have been continued by the banks on my undertaking to introduce the present measure at this session.
4.	To limit the liability of the government under the guarantee to a maximum of $300 million which may be lent by all banks collectively during the new lending period. As I have mentioned previously, the contingent liability of the government with respect to the lending was limited, in the lending period which recently ended, to a total of $300 million lent by all banks. That is to say, the liability is based on 10 per cent of the lending of each individual chartered bank up to a total lent by all banks of $300 million. In the period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1959 there was approximately $240 million lent by all the banks and consequently it is felt that the $300 million figure is likely to be adequate for the servicing of this credit for the period proposed, namely from April 1, 1959 to June 30, 1962.

I think the committee generally will welcome the announcement of the minister. I was particularly pleased to hear the tributes which the hon. gentleman paid to this particular statute, the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This was one of the many statutes which were made available or which were created after the war to take care of the economic transition which was expected to take place at that time.
Unfortunately, members of the committee have not available too much information. I do not say that this is a new situation. The last time we were asked to amend the act in 1956 we were asked to do so for another expiry date, and legislation was introduced in March of that year, 1956, when there was more excuse for not having available to the House of Commons the latest report for the calendar year. I find that my remarks must be somewhat limited by the fact that the latest report available to members of the House of Commons is the report for loans made under the act for 1957.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement a convention between Canada and Finland for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to taxes on income. As hon. members are aware, the bill is in the same form, and the convention it is intended to ratify is in the same form, as others which have been before the house in recent years. The substance of the convention follows the general pattern of the income tax conventions which Canada has entered into with the United States, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, France, Sweden, Ireland, Denmark, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Union of South Africa, the Netherlands, Australia and Belgium. All of those were, in their turn, swiftly approved by the house.
In particular, the provisions of this convention are similar to those in the convention between Canada and Denmark. I have no doubt, therefore, a general account of the terms of the convention will suffice for present purposes.

The main purpose of the convention is to avoid double taxes on income of persons both individual and corporate, who are resident in one of the countries and receive income from the other country. The taxes included in the scope of the convention are the Canadian federal income tax, including surtaxes, and the old age security tax on income and the Finnish national income tax. As in Canada, this tax applies to the income of both individuals and corporations. There is no equivalent in Finland of Canada's old age security tax on income.
The chief means of avoiding double taxation is by a reciprocal system of tax credits where the country of residence gives credit for the tax imposed by the country where the income has its source.
Another means is by providing that in certain instances the country in which the income has its source is not to impose tax on that income. In this case it will be taxed only once-by the country of residence. This rule applies to the following kinds of income: Profits on shipping and aircraft companies; copyright royalties from certain artistic activities; purchased annuities; pensions paid in consideration of past services, and business profits not derived through a permanent establishment. In some instances it also applies to the remuneration for personal services rendered by visitors who are businessmen, members of professions, professors, teachers, students and apprentices.
Double taxation is also reduced by restricting to a maximum rate of 15 per cent the withholding tax on certain income going from one country to the residents of the other. It is reduced also by the prohibition of discriminatory taxes against citizens of the other country and by the provision for settlement of special cases of double taxation by mutual agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to introduce a bill entitled the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act that will revise and re-enact part V of the Defence Services Pension Act.
The Defence Services Pension Act, as hon. members know, is divided into five parts. Parts I to IV apply only to persons who were enrolled in the regular forces prior to March 31, 1946. Part V applies to those persons enrolled in the regular forces since March 31, 1946 and those enrolled before that date who had elected to come under part V.
The pension schemes under parts I to IV and part V are basically the same. The principal difference is that under parts I to IV an other rank, that is a non-commissioned officer or man, contributes nothing to the pension fund but has no pension protection for his widow or dependent children. Under

those parts officers contribute 5 per cent of their pay and allowances to the pension fund. Under part V both officers and other ranks are required to contribute 6 per cent of their pay and allowances and all officers and other ranks have protection for their widows and dependent children. Under both pension schemes the amount of the pension is one-fiftieth of pay and allowances for each year of service. The pay and allowances under parts I to IV are based on the average of the last three years' service; under part V they are based on the average of the last six years. Under the new act parts I to IV basically stand and only very few minor amendments are made. Part V is repealed and replaced by the new act.
The new act will not deprive anyone now serving in the forces of any of his substantial pension rights. The principal purpose of the new act is to simplify administration, correct certain anomalies and bring the regular forces' pension scheme into greater conformity with the Public Service Superannuation Act and the proposed new Royal Canadian Mounted Police superannuation act, the resolution of which was introduced this afternoon.
Whilst the basic pension scheme of part V of the Defence Services Pension Act is retained in the proposed new act, the following important changes will be made. Men who are granted commissions for a fixed term of service will cease to be contributors under this act; they will receive a gratuity under the act for their service as a man and a gratuity under deferred pay regulations in respect of their commissioned time. This will obviate the payment of pensions to relatively young men. Officers who are permitted to retire voluntarily and have 25 years' regular service will be eligible to receive a pension reduced by 5 per cent for each year under their retirement age. Previously they only had to serve 20 years. The maximum benefits payable to widows and children will be raised to those contained in the Public Service Superannuation Act; that is to say, from a maximum of 75 per cent of the contributor's pension to 90 per cent. Only a return of contributions will be payable in future except in the case of death or disability of a contributor where he has served three years or less in the regular forces. Members of the forces to whom parts I to IV of the Defence Services Pension Act are applicable will be given one more year within which to elect to come under the new statute. This will permit men under parts I to IV to obtain protection for their families. The proposed new
Defence Services Pension Act act will be very similar to the Public Service Superannuation Act which was enacted by parliament in 1953.

The fact remains, however, that additional amendments have been found necessary since 1955 and these seem to point to the need for a much more thorough going review of this act than has yet taken place-

*-it seems to me we have reached the limit of absurdity when we ask the workers of this country to put up more money to solve the unemployment situation. That is the government's job, not the workers.

It seems obvious to us that, of late years, the Canadian government has been inclined to have the unemployment insurance fund assume certain expenses which normally should be paid from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, or by special social security measures. We believe that the rather rapid decrease in the level of the fund is much more the result of that policy than a consequence of inadequate contributions by employees and employers in relation to normal costs incurred by the administration of the act.
That is why we fully support the Unemployment Insurance Commission's advisory committee recommendation to raise the government's contribution to a satisfactory level in order to cover the cost of unemployment insurance elements which have been introduced in the legislation. That government's contribution should be at least half the overall contributions of both employers and employees.
Finally, for the reasons we pointed out in the above paragraphs, we are opposed to the proposed contribution increase. In our opinion, it is unwarranted and saddles the insured with a financial burden which should be taken care of by another fund than the unemployment insurance.
Here now is a brief submitted by the Canadian Retail Federation, which says: (Text):
Generally speaking, it seems to us that government has two means at its disposal to ease the effects of unemployment both in regard to the individual unemployed and to the economy of the country.
One is a scheme of unemployment insurance based on sound actuarial principles and designed to pay out benefits to those insured persons who become unemployed. The other is a program of public assistance designed to provide for those not protected at all or not protected adequately by unemployment insurance and to assist in those periodic times of economic recession during which unemployment rises to abnormal heights.
Unemployment Insurance Act We do not criticize the humanitarian motives of government in making changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act, intended to cope with such problems as those produced by seasonality in economic activity, by industries that are essentially seasonal in character, or by economic recession with its attendant and often substantial degree of unemployment which may be of considerable duration. We are intensely concerned to see what we believe to be undue and even unfair demands made upon the unemployment insurance fund, demands which appear to violate the actuarial basis of a good insurance act and which pertain rather to a program of public assistance than to a sound insurance scheme.
The results of such mingling on any wide scale of the two concepts of unemployment insurance and public assistance are only too likely to be reflected in an unsound fund, an effect which seems to be already unfortunately in evidence.
In the act as it now stands this discrimination against the main body of supporting contributors appears to have occurred to a considerable degree.
For example, in covering the employee in stable, year-round work the risk involved is unexpected unemployment, but with highly seasonal industries the risk is expected unemployment during some part of each year. Unless the highly seasonal industries are protected under some other legislation, it would appear that only higher rates for them, in recognition of a greater risk, can avoid the effect of subsidization by both employers and employees in the more stable industries. Lack of recognition of this would seem to involve unfair discrimination against the bulk of contributors who may reasonably expect their contributions to be used to cover the contingency of their unexpected unemployment.
Summary and Recommendations
(3) The federation recommends that a royal commission or similar body be established to completely review the Unemployment Insurance Act.

We find that in March 1958, the unemployment insurance fund had assets of $744,200,124.87, while in March 1959 the amount was down to $496,251,386.48. This means, Mr. Chairman, that as a result of the recession we have been through, considerable amounts from this fund have had to be paid to the

Unemployment Insurance Act unemployed, at the expense of people who had paid contributions in the hope that they might benefit in the event of their becoming temporarily unemployed in the course of their lifetime. I think the government is seriously derelict in its duty if it fails to take from the consolidated revenue fund the necessary money to put back the unemployment insurance fund on a sound basis. In such a case, the government will simply be holding two classes of society responsible for all the trouble we have been having in Canada for some time.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say something concerning these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I may say that I joined the committee rather late, and most of the briefs had been submitted. However, several briefs were presented, and those which I heard, as well as those which I read, were practically all critical of the amendments that have been presented.
In looking over the briefs I find most of them are against the rise in the contributions or against the fund paying the supplementary benefits, more particularly the seasonal benefits. They recommend that the whole matter should be referred to a committee of actuaries who would devise some better methods than those contained in these particular amendments. Labour, for the most part, agreed with the increases in benefits and the extension of benefits from 36 to 52 weeks. However, they objected greatly to paying contributions out of all proportion to the cost of these increased benefits. So far as I can see, the government has paid no attention to these recommendations that were received by the committee through the different briefs that were submitted.
I know the government has a big majority, and they will probably carry through this measure. However, I believe they should listen to some of the advice that has been given, and some of the representations made, particularly from employers and from labour. From the manufacturers' point of view, these amendments certainly add to their cost of production in a highly competitive market. It is difficult for many of our manufacturers to maintain themselves in some products even in our home market. When their costs rise,


this rise will tend to increase unemployment even further. To give you some examples of what the manufacturers think of these amendments, I have only to refer to one presentation which is typical of several that were submitted. They say this:
The present wording of the act with reference to eligibility qualifications has many ambiguities which make it extremely difficult for the local offices to prevent abuses.
I might say that I can refer to this particular reference in some of the labour representations. The manufacturers also state as follows:
The extension of the plan in recent years whereby additional occupational groups of employees have been included and by which benefit periods were increased in length has thrown the unemployment insurance fund into jeopardy . . .
The scheme has departed from its original concept of an actuarially sound insurance plan designed to tide employees over periods of temporary unemployment. Generally speaking, the operating deficits in recent years may be attributed to the above-mentioned extensions of both coverage and benefits.
One has only to go to the representation made by the Canadian Congress of Labour to see what they say about these amendments. They say this:
We think that the fund, to the extent that it needs replenishing through means other than a return to full employment, should be replenished in other ways and from other sources.
They make certain recommendations. They say:
The congress believes that there are other amendments which should be made to the act. We have already referred to the need for much greater coverage than now exists, more particularly to the justification of immediate inclusion of hospital employees.
Being connected with some hospitals, I might say that I think that hospital employees across Canada, or at least those in the part of Canada in which I live, would like the opportunity of being included under this act. The paragraph continues:
Other amendments that we recommend to you for your consideration are:
(1)	the elimination of the waiting period;
(2)	the elimination of the anomalies in regard to benefits during illness whereby benefit would be available if and as soon as employment was lost due to illness;
(3)	modification of the disqualification resulting from unemployment due to a stoppage of work whereby such disqualification would not result if the stoppage is a lockout imposed by the employer,-
Then they go on to recommend prohibition of referrals to struck plants; restoration of dependency status for dependents residing outside Canada and so on. I think I have referred to sufficient here to show that both labour and industry are opposed to the amendments proposed by the government.
In looking over the state of the fund, according to page one of the unemployment

insurance supplement that was issued, we find that at the end of the fiscal year 1957- that is at the end of March, 1957-the fund had $874 million and that at the end of the fiscal year 1959 the fund had $496 million, a drop of $378 million. According to the investment position changes tabled in the house the figure for government securities on hand as of March 31, 1959 was $490 million, down over $250 million from the previous March 31. As I was saying, Mr. Chairman-
I am waiting for hon. gentlemen to stop making remarks.
According to report No. 6 with regard to unemployment insurance, which was sent to

us by Department of Labour officials, the addition of two classes would cost the unemployment insurance commission $9,400,000, and the increase resulting from the 36 to 52 weeks' extension of the benefit period would amount to $11 million. The adjustment would equal $3,100,000, which brings the total of new expenses for the unemployment insurance commission to $23,500,000.
When it is known that a 30 per cent increase would represent an amount of $78 million, while new expenses are supposed to amount to no more than $23,500,000, we can well believe that there's something wrong in the way this act was put together.
Besides, if losses had occurred simply because the commission had had to pay somewhat more to keep the jobless provided with the basic necessities of life, we might understand the situation. But we have been told that the unemployment insurance commission was advised by the investment committee to exchange a number of securities it held for long term conversion bonds, which resulted in a 10 million dollar loss. However, that figure does not represent the actual value of those bonds, which has been reduced to the extent that, if we were forced to sell those we own, in order to obtain enough money to pay the people who need unemployment insurance benefits, the commission would have to take an additional loss of $62 million, which added to the $10 million, gives a total of $72 million, i.e. approximately the amount needed to replenish the fund which has been depleted for the last few years.
Mr. Chairman, the worker and the employer should not be called upon to shoulder the total cost of the damages brought about by a somewhat faulty administration, because I understand there was incompatibility between the chairman of the investment committee and the one who acted as adviser for the unemployment insurance commission. In fact, the latter was caught in an extraordinary dilemma, as he was at the same time adviser to the Minister of Finance, in which capacity he advised him to issue a conversion loan. On the other hand, on account of the secret he had to keep, he could not advise the unemployment insurance commission that there was some risk in keeping any longer the treasury bills which it still had in hand and that it would be preferable to sell them on the market to get a better price. So, the commission kept its treasury bills till the last moment, which led to the exchange for conversion bonds, and to that considerable loss. Furthermore, unemployment had increased enormously. Now, instead of buying treasury bills which could have been sold on the market when they would have brought

more money, the unemployment insurance commission was practically forced to accept long term bonds in order to give the Minister of Finance the credit of having made a marvellous deal. On the other hand, we know that certain other public bodies having bonds sold them in time and did not incur the losses incurred by the unemployment insurance commission. Furthermore, those losses were caused by an urgent need of money, brought about by the need for paying unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Chairman, according to the table I have here the percentage of outlays compared to revenues in 1952 was but 44.2 per cent; in 1953, that percentage was 64.9; in 1954, 86.3; in 1955, 118.7; in 1956, it was back to 94.1; in 1957, to 91.9 and in 1958, to 151.2; finally, in 1959, it reached 207.5.
Mr. Chairman, this means that employers and employees are now being taxed for the administration's mistakes, whereas the money should be drawn from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
We note that in 1958, employer and employee contributions amounted to $718,409.64, while the government's share was $143,681.93. In 1959, the share of employees and employers will be $778,008.07, while the government's share will be raised to only $155,601.41. This means that there is a drop in the share to be paid by the government as compared to the share that employees and employers are being forced to pay.
Mr. Chairman, when we look at the bill, we find that there are certainly some items we can accept. However, we cannot see how the government can introduce this bill and ask us to pass it, and take advantage of its majority to push it through, when all public organizations we have heard are unanimous in objecting to the bill as it reads. Despite this disapproval, the government apparently intends to ram it down the throats of the Canadian people.
If objections had come only from labour organizations, I would say that perhaps they are a little biased, but we find that not only the workers, but employers, chambers of commerce, manufacturers and builders throughout Canada have all, without exception, objected to the bill, that all have described it as impractical and have suggested that it be studied by a special committee or by a royal commission appointed by the government. And when we ask that the bill be postponed out of deference for the wishes of the great majority of people in every part of Canada, they say "we want to help the workers". Yet when we suggested that at the beginning of this session the house adjourn for the purpose of studying the unemploy-
TJnemployment Insurance Act ment situation, the government objected that there was no urgency at the time, although there were 500,000 unemployed in Canada. There was no urgency! But today when, according to them, the number of unemployed has decreased, they want to put through legislation which is not practical and which will please no one. Besides, when we asked for information in order to study this legislation, it was refused to us.
On several occasions, in order to be able to have a good understanding of this bill, we asked for certain information which, by the way had been printed in the newspapers, but was never given officially in the house, at the committee, they took pleasure in putting grit in the bearings, almost continually.
Mr. Chairman, I could take any report from the committee and show you that we were discriminated against, because they did not want the truth to come out. We were repeatedly insulted because we asked for information that the government was not ready to give out. At this stage, I want to be fair and say that when he appeared before the committee, the minister gave us enough leeway and answered our questions fairly well. However, we were not allowed to seek advice from the unemployment insurance advisory committee whose members were in a position to give us plenty of information on that question, since the advisory committee had not recommended that measure. Despite the fact that the advisory committee put forward the same reasons as those submitted by the various public organizations, the government is bent anyway on by-passing those suggestions and intends to thrust that bill upon us.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that the attitude shown, at the industrial relations committee meetings, toward members of the Liberal party and C.C.F. members present is a glaring injustice. Every time a question was asked, the chairman rose and declared it out of order, even before we had a chance to express an opinion.
He led the discussions of this committee in a deplorable way and prevented us from obtaining the information we needed to debate the matter further in the house.

Mr. Chairman, those interjections indicate that our complaints are justified.
I was going to suggest to the Minister of Labour whose responsibility it is to recommend members to be appointed chairmen of various committees, that if he intends again to recommend the appointment of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small) as chairman of the industrial relations committee next year, he should set up a special class in order that the hon. member may get acquainted with parliamentary procedure and the way to preside at meetings. In fact, twice we had to leave the meeting in protest, because we were being denied the required information, and this as a result of the line followed by the hon. member for Danforth who was chairman of the committee. Therefore, we missed part of those sittings and the opportunity was taken to rush things through.
Mr. Chairman, I referred a while ago to labour representatives who appeared before the committee to present their views. This advisory committee included labour representatives who had to resign because they did not agree with the way the government was dealing with Canadian workers. And when we discussed the situation, a certain member whose riding I do not recall said something like this:
(Text):
The resignation of the labour members has been a service to the commission.
[Mr. Ricard.l
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, these words could give the impression that the workers' representatives within the commission were not acting according to their conscience or in a way that would help the committee and advise the minister with insight and objectivity.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I contend that, at this time, we are not in a position to pass bill C-23, for lack of relevant information.
We received protests from organizations throughout the country. I believe that, as long as we have not received the necessary information which would enable us to consider the bill, we, in this house, cannot vote in favour of a legislation which can, at present, be considered unfair, because it throws upon only two groups of our society the whole burden of the errors that have possibly been committed by the present government since it has been managing this country's business and which may have been the cause of a decrease in our international trade and thus of a lack of employment in Canada.
This decline in our trade also caused some industries to close down, at least for a while. Warehouses were chock full of goods and manufacturers were being forced to stop production while waiting to sell part of the accumulated stock.
Mr. Chairman, if that is the government policy, there cannot be any doubt that the resulting unemployment is responsible for the deplorable condition of the unemployment fund. It rests with the government to replenish the unemployment fund. It is also up to the government to contribute $400 million to the fund, if necessary, so as to restore it to the level it was at before the economic recession, so that employees and employers shall not be requested to pay larger contributions into this fund which is designed to help those who lost their jobs, as a result of the difficult economic conditions which the country has been facing these last few years.
Mr. Chairman, I urge the minister to adjourn the debate on that measure and to set up a committee to study it further. I am satisfied that in acting upon this suggestion, it would be granting the request of the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian manufacturers, the Board of Trade of Canada, the Chamber of Commerce, the Board of Trade of Toronto, and of all who appeared before the committee. Then we will be In a position to draft a bill more suited to the needs of the country, of the worker and of

the employer, because, and we should not forget it, as a result of the proposed increase of the contributions, certain industries which produce particular items will see their production cost increased by as much as $16,000 a year. That fact was brought to the attention of the committee on industrial relations by the Canadian manufacturers.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, can we reasonably require that only two categories of people in Canada be responsible for all the troubles that this country is experiencing today? Can the minister logically attempt to keep on imposing on us such a measure when he personally knows that the advisory committee, far from recommending it, even criticized it?
Can he logically ask this house to pass it, unless he uses a servile majority to force it upon us.
I say that we propose to fight it. We are trying to get the minister to allow us at least the time to go into it more thoroughly. Meanwhile, let the government, which is responsible for that sorry plight, pay out of Canada's consolidated revenue fund the amount required to replenish the unemployment insurance fund, because we know that if next winter we have anything like last winter's unemployment, it will cost at least another $250 million. And in view of the fact that there is only some $350 million left at the present time and that the market value is lower than the book value, it is my contention that if we have that kind of unemployment next winter, the fund will practically be exhausted and the government will have yet to draw from the consolidated revenue fund to maintain conditions across the country.
So, if the government, by reason of the dangerous state of the fund, has to draw additional amounts from the consolidated revenue fund, why should it not do it right now? Then it could have this bill studied by an independent body, which could be made up of persons having made special economic studies who could advise the government. If their views were similar to that of the advisory committee, that would mean that the government would be in the wrong, and then we would vote against the bill. If, on the other hand, that particular committee advised the government to follow its present policy, well, we could say to the government: assume your own responsibilities. We would let the bill go through with
Unemployment Insurance Act all the more satisfaction since it would have been thoroughly examined.
There are things which are not accurate in this bill. For instance, it is claimed that the increase will average 30 per cent. But when we consider the new classes, we realize that the increase will reach 64 per cent in certain cases. An increase of 64 per cent, both for the worker and for the employer, means an increase in the cost of living. An increase in the cost of living means an inflationary upsurge in the country. An inflationary upsurge in the country means that the cost of our goods will increase to such an extent that we are going to go on losing our markets abroad. And if we keep on losing our markets abroad, there will be an increase in the number of unemployed in Canada.
Can we afford, here in Canada, a small country in terms of population but large in size, to wait until that calamity is upon us before we react? I say that the ministers are too responsible to accept such a view. I say, as the Minister of Finance did say himself, that we must assess the situation and check that increase, in order that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) may find markets for the products we have at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, we want the minister to change his mind and grant us a more detailed study of the bill before it is adopted.
